source.version: Author accepted manuscript for Computers & Education, dated March 9th, 2024. The boxed notice on p. 1 says it is not the copy of record and gives the final article's DOI, 10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031. Per retrieval.json, this file is the PsyArXiv posting (10.31234/osf.io/9z2tc, OSF file version 3, uploaded 2024-03-18), and retrieval found no differences in studies or sample from the journal version of record (Computers & Education 215, 105031), which is not on file. Printed page numbers match the PDF page index.
source.title_on_document: ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study

supplement.where: None referenced. The manuscript cites no supplementary material, online appendix, data, or code (pp. 1-40 read). Its only appendix, Appendix 1 (evaluation matrix for the Product Improvement Task, adapted from Todd et al. 2019), is printed in this PDF on p. 40. The only external link is the preregistration, osf.io/q6wtu (p. 9).
supplement.holds: Nothing outside this PDF. Appendix 1 holds the rating rubric and example answers, no statistics. All arm means, SDs, t-tests, and d values are in Table 2 (p. 16); the ANCOVA and interaction F-tests are in the text (pp. 16-17). The paper prints no standard errors and no numeric confidence intervals.

paper_design_summary: A preregistered lab experiment randomly assigned university student volunteers to solve a Product Improvement Task (three ideas to improve a stuffed bunny so that Mattel outsells the Lego Group) either with ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) open in a second browser tab (77 students analyzed) or without it (68 analyzed), with no exclusions. Both groups first did an Unusual Uses Task without ChatGPT as a baseline. Two experts blind to condition rated each participant's solutions for quality, elaboration, and originality on 1-5 scales, and the paper also reports self-rated self-efficacy, self-evaluations, interest, difficulty, and effort.

studies.label: Lab experiment: Product Improvement Task with vs. without ChatGPT

assignment.what_was_assigned: Solving the Product Improvement Task with ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) open in a second browser tab (experimental condition) or without ChatGPT (control condition). Before the PIT, the experimental condition also read a brief description of ChatGPT with example prompts and responses (p. 10) and answered eight self-efficacy items, four without and four with ChatGPT, where the control answered four (p. 13).
assignment.quote: Male and female students who volunteered for the experiment were randomly assigned to either the control condition (task resolution without ChatGPT) or the experimental one (task resolution with ChatGPT) prior to the experiment.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 9, end of Present Study: 'The experimental design and research hypotheses were preregistered at Open Science Framework (osf.io/q6wtu).'

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Solved the PIT with ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) open in a second browser tab, after a brief description of ChatGPT with example prompts and responses. The task instructions added '[With the assistance of ChatGPT,]'. Its sessions were separate from the control group's (p. 10).

arms.name: Control (no ChatGPT)
arms.description: Solved the same PIT in a single open browser tab, with no other open tabs and no ChatGPT. Students in both conditions were free to use the browser for other tools, but the paper says no one did (p. 10).

participants.exclusions: None. 'All the participants passed the attention checks and completed all the required tasks. Therefore, no participants were excluded.' (p. 10). The paper gives arm sizes (68 control, 77 experimental; p. 11, Table 1) but no count at assignment. Volunteers were assigned 'prior to the experiment', and the paper does not say whether any assigned volunteer failed to attend, so n_randomized stays null. The Table 2 t-tests have df 143 and the ANCOVAs F(1,142), which match 145 analyzed.
participants.who: University student volunteers from a pool of approx. 8000 students, emailed under the general title 'Creative Thinking', who received a small portion of a course credit (pp. 9-10). Table 1: control 22 male and 46 female, mean age 22.5 (SD 4.9), 52 social sciences and humanities, 9 life sciences, 7 technical subjects, 55 BA and 13 MA; experimental 24 male and 53 female, mean age 22.4 (SD 4.1), 57, 17, and 3 by subject, 53 BA and 24 MA (p. 11). The paper says the sample was homogenous in race and ethnicity.
participants.country: Czech Republic. This paper names no country, but its lab was at the first author's institution (p. 9), which p. 1 lists as the Institute of Psychology, The Czech Academy of Sciences, Prague, Czech Republic, and both arms came from one pool of volunteers (p. 9). c594, which analyzes the 77 experimental participants, says they came from 'a large university in Prague, Czech Republic' (c594 preprint p. 9).
participants.quote: The control group for the present study contained 68 university students and the experimental group contained 77 participants
participants.locator: p. 11, Participants and Table 1; no exclusions p. 10; abstract p. 2; country from p. 9 and p. 1, with c594 preprint p. 9

ai_tool.how_used: A second browser tab with ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) was open during the PIT. Before the PIT, participants read a brief description of ChatGPT with example prompts and responses and were told that ChatGPT responds to prompts, that prompts need detail, and that they could add context or ask ChatGPT to regenerate its responses (p. 10). The PIT text was the same in both arms except one phrase. In the experimental condition, its last paragraph, the instruction sentence at the top of p. 13, opened with '[With the assistance of ChatGPT,]'. The two Mattel scenario paragraphs on p. 12 carry no added text (pp. 12-13). This paper reports no data on how participants used ChatGPT (prompts, number of queries, or logs), only a self-rated usefulness of ChatGPT (Table 2 row 14), and does not say whether use was logged. c594, which analyzes the same 77 participants, says that all of them engaged with ChatGPT during the task, although the instructions did not make its use mandatory, and it codes their conversation transcripts (c594 preprint pp. 9-11).

task.description: Product Improvement Task adapted from Puente-Díaz et al. (2021): as a consultant hired by Mattel, create three solutions to improve an ordinary stuffed bunny, about 30 cm in size, that are as original and as useful as possible to help Mattel achieve higher sales than the Lego Group (pp. 12-13). It followed an Unusual Uses Task (paperclip), done without ChatGPT in both arms as a baseline (pp. 10, 12).
task.duration: Whole experiment M = 26 (SD = 8) minutes in the control condition and M = 36 (SD = 9) minutes in the experimental condition (p. 10). No time limit for the PIT is stated.

outcomes.name: PIT quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two experts, blind to condition, independently rated the PIT answers, presented in randomized order. Quality is 'the extent to which the answers match the goals provided (i.e., to improve the bunny and to increase sales)', rated from 1 (worst) to 5 (best) with the matrix in Appendix 1 (p. 40); weighted kappa quality = .88 (p. 13). The paper names its experts as the first and last authors in the UUT paragraph (p. 12) but does not restate who rated the PIT or how the two PIT ratings were combined. Preregistered hypothesis H1a (pp. 8-9). Variants: independent-samples t-test (Table 2) and ANCOVA with prior ChatGPT experience as covariate (p. 16).

contrasts.reported: Table 2, '4. PIT (quality)': Control M = 2.99 (SD 0.86, N = 68) vs Experimental M = 3.60 (SD 0.89, N = 77); t(143) = 4.16, p < .001, d = 0.69. ANCOVA (covariate: prior ChatGPT experience): F(1,142) = 19.07, p <.001, partial eta squared = .12.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Table 2 row 4 and H1 text; Ns from p. 11, Table 1

outcomes.name: PIT elaboration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same two blind experts rated elaboration, which 'is measured by the amount of detail', from 1 (worst) to 5 (best) with Appendix 1 (p. 40); weighted kappa elaboration = .93 (p. 13). Preregistered hypothesis H1b (pp. 8-9). Variants: independent-samples t-test (Table 2) and ANCOVA with prior ChatGPT experience as covariate (p. 16).

contrasts.reported: Table 2, '5. PIT (elaboration)': Control M = 2.21 (SD 0.74, N = 68) vs Experimental M = 2.79 (SD 1.11, N = 77); t(143) = 3.65, p < .001, d = 0.61. ANCOVA (covariate: prior ChatGPT experience): F(1,142) = 14.87, p = <.001, partial eta squared = .10.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Table 2 row 5 and H1 text; Ns from p. 11, Table 1

outcomes.name: PIT originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same two blind experts rated originality, which 'represents the uniqueness of the ideas', from 1 (worst) to 5 (best) with Appendix 1 (p. 40); weighted kappa originality = .85 (p. 13). Preregistered hypothesis H1c (pp. 8-9). Variants: independent-samples t-test (Table 2); ANCOVA with prior ChatGPT experience as covariate (p. 16); and a group x task interaction on z-scored originality, with the UUT (done without ChatGPT in both arms) as pre-test and the PIT as the experimental task (Figure 1, p. 17). Figure 1 draws 95% CI error bars on the z-scored arm means and prints no interval values.

contrasts.reported: Table 2, '6. PIT (originality)': Control M = 2.21 (SD 0.91, N = 68) vs Experimental M = 2.74 (SD 1.02, N = 77); t(143) = 3.32, p < .001, d = 0.55. ANCOVA (covariate: prior ChatGPT experience): F(1,142) = 12.56, p < .001, partial eta squared = .08. Figure 1 (z-scored originality, pre-test UUT vs PIT): pre-test difference F(1,142) = 0.01, p = .928, partial eta squared = .00; interaction F(1,142) = 7.79, p = .006, partial eta squared = .05. The z-score means and their 95% CI error bars appear only in the figure.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Table 2 row 6 and H1 text; p. 17, Figure 1 and text below it; Ns from p. 11, Table 1

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Urban et al. (2025), 'Prompting for creative problem-solving: A process-mining study', Learning and Instruction 99, 102156 (atlas candidate c594). It analyzes the 77 experimental-arm participants of this study: the coded transcripts of their ChatGPT conversations and the expert ratings of their PIT solutions, with the same weighted kappas (.88, .93, .85). It has no no-AI arm. Its sample description matches this paper's Table 1 experimental column on N, sex (24 men, 53 women), mean age (22.4), study subject (57, 17, 3), and level (53 undergraduates, 24 graduates), but it prints age SD 4.5 where Table 1 prints 4.1. This PDF predates c594 and names no other paper that uses its sample. Codebook section 2 gives the two papers one sample. c594 is not in retrieval.json and was read in its PsyArXiv preprint, not its journal version.

sample_overlap.locator: c594 preprint, PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/68fh4 v3 (file 'ChatGPT process mining_PREPRINT_V3_Urban et al..pdf', posted 2025-05-06), p. 9, Methods, Participants; ratings and transcripts pp. 10-11; journal version 10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102156 not checked; this PDF p. 11, Table 1 (c594 is not this PDF)

company_involvement.description: No company involvement. The manuscript has no funding, acknowledgment, or conflict-of-interest statement (pp. 1-40 read). ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) is the tool studied; Mattel and the Lego Group appear only in the hypothetical task scenario.

eligibility.reason: Volunteers were randomly assigned as individuals to solve an idea-generation task with or without ChatGPT (p. 10). 145 people were analyzed, 77 with ChatGPT and 68 without, with no exclusions (pp. 10-11, Table 1), well above 50. Two experts blind to condition rated the quality, elaboration, and originality of the solutions, which the experimental arm produced with ChatGPT open (pp. 10, 13; Table 2, p. 16). c594 reuses the 77 experimental participants in a study with no no-AI arm, which changes none of the three criteria.

one_line_finding: Students randomly assigned to solve the Product Improvement Task with ChatGPT received higher expert ratings than students without it on quality (3.60 vs 2.99, d = 0.69), elaboration (2.79 vs 2.21, d = 0.61), and originality (2.74 vs 2.21, d = 0.55), all p < .001 (77 vs 68 students analyzed; means, d, and p in Table 2, p. 16; Ns in Table 1, p. 11).
open_questions: Conditions ran in separate sessions of up to five people ('The control group and experimental groups had separate sessions', p. 10), so session is confounded with condition. Students were randomly assigned as individuals before the experiment, but the paper does not say how sessions were scheduled, and its t-tests and ANCOVAs treat participants as independent.

The paper gives arm sizes (68 and 77) but no count at assignment and no randomization mechanism, and it does not say whether any assigned volunteer failed to attend. c594, which describes only the 77 experimental participants, gives no count at assignment either.

No outcome is named primary. Quality, elaboration, and originality are the preregistered sub-hypotheses H1a-c (p. 8), with no ranking among them. The preregistration (osf.io/q6wtu) was not checked in this reconciliation.

For the PIT, the paper does not say who the two experts were or how their two ratings became one score. Both facts are stated only for the UUT baseline, which the first and last authors rated and averaged (p. 12). c594 says only that 'two independent experts' rated the responses (c594 preprint p. 10).

The rubric in Appendix 1 (p. 40) does not say whether one score covers a participant's three solutions or each solution is scored and then averaged. The df of 143 imply one score per participant, and the top elaboration level ('all three solutions are connected in a single coherent narrative') suggests the whole response was scored. c594, describing the same ratings, says the experts 'assessed the quality, elaboration, and originality of each idea' (c594 preprint p. 10), so the point stays open.

The treatment is a bundle: the experimental arm also read a ChatGPT introduction with example prompts and answered four extra self-efficacy items before the PIT (pp. 10, 13), and it took longer overall (M = 36 vs 26 minutes, p. 10).

Use of ChatGPT is answered outside this paper. This paper reports no usage data and does not say whether every experimental participant used ChatGPT. c594, which analyzes the same 77 participants, says 'all participants engaged with it during the task' and codes their conversation transcripts (c594 preprint pp. 9-11). The contrast in this form stays by assigned condition.

This is the accepted manuscript. The journal version of record (Computers & Education 215, 105031) is not on file and may add a data availability, funding, or conflict-of-interest statement that this PDF lacks.
notes: Outcomes not listed. The UUT baseline originality is a pre-treatment measure: both arms produced it first, without ChatGPT and before the ChatGPT introduction (p. 10), so it answers none of the three questions. Table 2 row 1: Control 1.74 (SD 0.99) vs Experimental 1.71 (SD 0.81), t(143) = 0.18, p = .855, d = 0.03 (p. 16); pre-test difference F(1,142) = 0.01, p = .928, partial eta squared = .00 (p. 17); rated by the first and last authors, weighted kappa = .80, one score as the mean of both judgments (p. 12). It enters S1-O3 only as the pre-test of the Figure 1 interaction. Self-reports are left out because they are not scored on the output: self-efficacy without and with ChatGPT, self-evaluations of quality and originality, interest, difficulty, effort, and usefulness of ChatGPT (Table 2 rows 2-3, 7-8, 11-14). The bias indices (rows 9-10) subtract rescaled expert scores from self-evaluations (p. 14), so they measure self-evaluation accuracy, not creativity: quality 0.04 (SD 0.32) vs 0.02 (SD 0.29), p = .694; originality 0.14 (SD 0.29) vs 0.09 (SD 0.35), p = .371. Prior ChatGPT experience, the ANCOVA covariate, had small effects on quality (F(1,142) = 4.00, p = .047), elaboration (F(1,142) = 3.95, p = .049), and originality (F(1,142) = 4.44, p = .037), each partial eta squared = .03 (p. 16). Table 3 (p. 18) gives correlations within each group. An a priori power analysis asked for at least 57 participants per group (p. 11). No outcome is named primary; under codebook section 8, rule 2, the primary with_ai record would be originality (S1-O3, novelty rated by experts), because the paper has no overall creativity rating. No diversity outcome and no outcome after AI was removed are reported: participants solved only the UUT, before the manipulation, and the PIT. The markdown conversion covers all 40 pages, through Appendix 1 on p. 40, and was read in full. All numbers were checked against the PDF page images (pp. 9-17 and 40). c594 (Urban et al. 2025) reuses the 77 experimental participants; see sample_overlap. This file replaces an earlier reconciled version built from earlier raw forms, which coded the three outcomes preregistered_primary and numbered originality S1-O1. This version follows both current screeners: outcome order quality, elaboration, originality, and primary = not_stated.

open_items.item: Sessions by condition (open question 1): each condition ran in its own sessions of up to five people, so session is confounded with condition, and the paper does not say how sessions were scheduled. Individual random assignment before the experiment is stated (p. 10), so criterion 1 holds. If sessions were the assigned unit, standard errors would need clustering (codebook section 10), which bears on pooling, not eligibility.

Assignment counts (open question 2): no count at assignment, no randomization mechanism, and no statement on no-shows, here or in c594. Random assignment is stated and 145 people were analyzed (each arm above 50), so criteria 1 and 2 hold either way.

Primary outcome (open question 3): the paper names none among quality, elaboration, and originality (H1a-c). The OSF preregistration (osf.io/q6wtu), not opened in this screening, may name one. Otherwise codebook section 8, rule 2 picks originality (S1-O3). Criterion 3 holds for all three outcomes.

PIT raters (open question 4): neither this paper nor c594 says who the two PIT experts were or how their two ratings became one score. Both raters were experts blind to condition, so criterion 3 holds either way.

Scoring unit (open question 5): whether one score covers each participant's three solutions or each solution is scored and averaged. The df of 143 put one score per participant in the analysis, so unit stays participant, while c594 says experts rated 'each idea'. Criterion 3 holds either way.

Treatment bundle (open question 6): the ChatGPT arm also read a ChatGPT introduction with example prompts and answered four extra self-efficacy items, and its sessions ran longer (36 vs 26 minutes). This is how the paper defines its treatment, and no other document would change it. Criterion 1 holds because access to ChatGPT was randomly assigned.

Use of ChatGPT (open question 7): this paper reports no usage data, but c594 says all 77 experimental participants engaged with ChatGPT and analyzes their transcripts. The contrast stays by assigned condition.

Version (open question 8): the version of record (Computers & Education 215, 105031) is not on file and may add data availability, funding, or conflict-of-interest statements. Retrieval found no differences in studies or sample.
